Problem 6.35, part (d) Lesson 25 · p. 359 · §6.3

DC analysis of a BJT circuit: find every terminal voltage and current, assuming a fixed base-emitter drop.

Problem statement

6.35 For each of the circuits shown in Fig. P6.35, find the emitter, base, and collector voltages and currents. Use β=50, but assume |VBE|=0.7 V independent of current level.

Assigned parts: (d). The book's figure shows all four circuits; the assigned one is circuit (d), at the lower right.

Similar to 6.35(d) same kind of circuit, new numbers · npn with a base voltage, collector and emitter resistors

Find the emitter, base and collector voltages and currents, then confirm the transistor really is in the active mode.

Similar problem (new numbers)

For the circuit below, find the emitter, base, and collector voltages and currents. Use β=80, but assume |VBE|=0.7 V independent of current level.

Step 1 · Base and emitter voltages

The base is held at VB=+2.0 V by the source. With the emitter-base junction forward biased, Table 6.3 gives VBE≃0.7 V, so

VE=VB−VBE=2.0−0.7=1.3V
Step 2 · Emitter current

Circuit rule (Ohm's law across RE, with the other end at ground):

IE=VE−0RE=1.31.5=0.867mA
Step 3 · Collector current

Assuming active mode, Table 6.2 gives iC=αiE with α=β/(β+1):

α=8081=0.988,IC=αIE=0.988×0.867=0.856mA
Step 4 · Collector voltage

Ohm's law across RC, from the supply:

VC=VCC−ICRC=6−0.856×3.3=3.18V
Step 5 · Base current

From Table 6.2, iB=iE/(β+1):

IB=IEβ+1=0.86781=0.0107mA=10.7μA

Check (KCL): IC+IB=0.856+0.011=0.867 mA, which equals IE.

Step 6 · Was active mode the right assumption?

For an npn transistor the collector-base junction is reverse biased as long as VC does not fall below VB by more than about 0.4 V (p. 321, p. 333):

VCB=VC−VB=3.18−2.0=+1.18V>−0.4V

The test is passed, so the active-mode model used in Steps 3 to 5 is consistent. As a second check, IC/IB=80=β.

Answers (similar problem)
VoltagesVB=2.0 V; VE=1.3 V; VC≈3.18 V
CurrentsIE≈0.867 mA; IC≈0.856 mA; IB≈10.7μA
ModeActive (VCB≈+1.18 V)

Expansion note: reading the type of transistor from the figure

The emitter is the terminal with the arrowhead. An arrow pointing out of the device (away from the base) marks an npn transistor; an arrow pointing into the device (toward the base) marks a pnp transistor. The type decides which way the currents flow and which of VBE or VEB is the positive junction voltage.

Lesson 25: where this problem sits Lesson 25 guide

Summarized

Lesson 25 covers BJT operation in the active mode, biasing and the small-signal model. This problem uses only the dc part: the large-signal active-mode relations and the procedure of assuming a mode and then checking it. The full lesson notes are in the Lesson 25 guide.

Circuit symbols and which junction is forward biased §6.2.1, pp. 319–321

Quoted · p. 320

The polarity of the device—npn or pnp—is indicated by the direction of the arrowhead. It points in the direction of normal current flow in the emitter, which is also the forward direction of the base-emitter junction. Since we have adopted a drawing convention by which currents flow from top to bottom, we will always draw pnp transistors with their emitters on top, as shown in Fig. 6.12(b).

Figure 6.13 shows npn and pnp transistors connected to dc sources so that they operate in the active mode. Figure 6.13 also shows the reference and actual directions of current flow throughout the transistor. Our convention is to take the reference direction to coincide with the normal direction of current flow. Normally, then, we should not encounter a negative value for iE, iB, or iC.

Quoted · pp. 320–321

From the discussion in Section 6.1 it follows that an npn transistor whose EBJ is forward biased (usually, vBE≃0.7 V) will operate in the active mode as long as the collector voltage does not fall below that of the base by more than approximately 0.4 V. Otherwise, the transistor leaves the active mode and enters the saturation region.

Expansion note: what "EBJ" and "CBJ" mean

A BJT has two junctions: the emitter-base junction (EBJ) and the collector-base junction (CBJ). Active mode means the EBJ is forward biased and the CBJ is reverse biased. Saturation means both are forward biased.

Active-mode current relations Table 6.2, p. 321

Expansion note: why alpha is close to 1

α=β/(β+1), so for β in the tens or hundreds, α is only slightly below 1. That is why the collector current and the emitter current are nearly equal while the base current is a small fraction of either.

Simplified dc models and the procedure for finding the mode Table 6.3 and §6.3, pp. 333–334
Quoted · p. 333

When analyzing a circuit, the first question we need to answer is: In which mode is the transistor operating? In some cases, the answer will be obvious. For instance, a quick check of the terminal voltages will indicate whether the transistor is cut off or conducting. If it is conducting, we have to determine whether it is in the active mode or in saturation. In some cases, it won't be obvious; with practice, however, it will become clear in more and more situations. Fortunately, we can always find the answer, using the following procedure.

Assume that the transistor is in the active mode and, using the active-mode model in Table 6.3, determine the various voltages and currents. Then, check for consistency of the results with the assumption of active-mode operation; in other words, is VCB of an npn transistor greater than −0.4 V (or VCB of a pnp transistor lower than 0.4 V)? If the answer is yes, then our task is complete. If the answer is no, assume saturation-mode operation and, using the saturation-mode model in Table 6.3, determine currents and voltages, and then check whether the results fit with the assumption of saturation-mode operation. Here the test is usually to compute the ratio IC/IB and verify that it is lower than the transistor β (i.e., βforced<β). For a given transistor type or part number, the manufacturer only gurantees β values will fall within a certain range, say 50 to 150. For this reason, we must use the lowest specified β for this test. Finally, note that the order of these two assumptions can be reversed.

Quoted · p. 334

A Note on Units Except when otherwise specified, throughout this book we use a consistent set of units, namely, volts (V), milliamps (mA), and kilohms (kΩ).

Expansion note: why the book says "assume, then check"

The two models in Table 6.3 behave differently, and you cannot tell from the circuit alone which one applies. So you pick one, calculate with it, and test whether the answers agree with that choice. A disagreement means the other model is the right one.

Worked example: analyzing a one-supply npn circuit Example 6.4, pp. 334–335

Quoted · Example 6.4 statement, p. 334

Consider the circuit in Fig. 6.23(a), which we have redrawn in Fig. 6.23(b) to remind you of the convention for indicating connections to dc sources. We want to analyze this circuit to determine all node voltages and branch currents. We will assume that β is specified to be 100.

Quoted · Example 6.4 solution, p. 335

Glancing at the circuit in Fig. 6.23(a), we see that the base is connected to +4 V and the emitter is connected to ground through a resistance RE. Therefore, it is reasonable to conclude that the base-emitter junction is forward biased. Assuming that this is the case and assuming that VBE is approximately 0.7 V, it follows that the emitter voltage is

VE=4−VBE≃4−0.7=3.3V

We are now in a good position: because we know the voltages at the two ends of RE, we can determine the current IE through it,

IE=VE−0RE=3.3V3.3kΩ=1mA

Since the collector is connected through RC to the +10-V power supply, it appears possible that the collector voltage will be higher than the base voltage, which implies active-mode operation. Assuming that this is the case, we can evaluate the collector current from

IC=αIE

The value of α is

α=ββ+1=100101≃0.99

Thus IC is given by

IC=0.99×1=0.99mA

We are now in a position to use Ohm's law to determine the collector voltage VC,

VC=10−ICRC=10−0.99×4.7≃+5.3V

Since the base is at +4 V, the collector-base junction is reverse biased by 1.3 V, and the transistor is indeed in the active mode as we assumed.

It remains only to determine the base current IB, as follows:

IB=IEβ+1=1101≃0.01mA

Before leaving this example, we want to strongly emphasize the value of carrying out the analysis directly on the circuit diagram. Only in this way will one be able to analyze complex circuits in a reasonable length of time. Figure 6.23(c) illustrates our analysis on the circuit diagram, with the order of the analysis steps indicated by the circled numbers.

Expansion note: reading the circled steps in Fig. 6.23(c)

The circled numbers give the order in which each quantity is found, working outward from the one node whose voltage is fixed by a source. Each step uses only quantities found in earlier steps.

When the active-mode assumption fails Examples 6.5 and 6.6, pp. 336–338

Summarized

Example 6.5 uses the same circuit as Example 6.4 with the base raised to +6 V. The active-mode calculation gives a collector voltage far below the base voltage, which contradicts the assumption. The book then re-solves with the saturation model of Table 6.3: VC=VE+VCEsat with VCEsat≃0.2 V, finds IC from the resistor between the supply and the collector, finds IB=IE−IC, and confirms that βforced=IC/IB is below the minimum specified β. It adds: “Remember to always use the minimum value of β when testing for saturation.”

Example 6.6 uses the same circuit with the base at 0 V. The emitter-base junction cannot conduct, so the transistor is in the cutoff mode: all currents are zero, the emitter is at 0 V and the collector is at the supply voltage.

Problem 16.5 Lesson 29 · p. 1145 · §16.1

Given a pull-down network, find the matching pull-up network, the complete CMOS gate and its Boolean function.

Problem statement

16.5 Find the PUN that corresponds to the PDN shown in Fig. P16.5, and hence the complete CMOS logic circuit. What is the Boolean function realized?

Similar to 16.5 given PDN, find the PUN, the whole gate and the function · §16.1

Same kind of question with a different pull-down network.

Similar problem (new network)

Find the PUN that corresponds to the PDN shown below, and hence the complete CMOS logic circuit. What is the Boolean function realized?

Step 1 · When does the PDN conduct?

An NMOS transistor conducts when its gate is high. In the PDN, devices in series form an AND and devices in parallel form an OR (p. 1114). The A-B branch conducts when A and B are both high; the C-D branch conducts when C and D are both high; either branch is enough, so the PDN conducts for

Y‾=AB+CD

because a conducting PDN pulls Y low.

Step 2 · The function
Y=AB+CD‾
Step 3 · Express Y with complemented variables

The PUN is built from PMOS devices, which conduct when the input is low, so it is easiest to write Y in terms of A‾, B‾, C‾, D‾. Apply DeMorgan's law as in Eq. (16.4):

Y=AB+CD‾=AB‾CD‾=(A‾+B‾)(C‾+D‾)
Step 4 · Read off the PUN

Y is high when (A low or B low) and (C low or D low). Parallel PMOS devices make the OR, and series connection of the two groups makes the AND. The same result follows from duality (§16.1.7): each series branch of the PDN becomes a parallel group in the PUN and the parallel arrangement becomes series.

Step 5 · Complete circuit

Join the PUN (between VDD and Y) and the PDN (between Y and ground) at the output node.

Check: for every input combination exactly one of the two networks conducts, so there is never a direct dc path from VDD to ground (p. 1113). This was confirmed for all 16 rows in the saved script. Counting devices: 4 NMOS + 4 PMOS = 8.

Answers (similar problem)
PUNTwo parallel PMOS pairs, (A,B) and (C,D), connected in series
Boolean functionY=AB+CD‾

Expansion note: the bar over a symbol

A bar over a symbol or expression means NOT: Y‾ is high when Y is low. A long bar over a whole expression, such as A+B‾, complements the entire expression, not each variable on its own; DeMorgan's law is the rule for moving the bar onto the variables.

Expansion note: "AND" and "OR" here describe conduction

The book says it directly: “Here, the OR and AND notations refer to current flow or conduction.” A series pair is an AND because both devices must be on for current to pass. The logic function of the whole gate is then found from whether the PDN conducts.

Lesson 29 notetaker: logic gates from PUN and PDN notetaker pp. 29-1 to 29-4

Summarized from the Lesson 29 notetaker

The notetaker opens with a recall of Lesson 28: a block of pull-up logic between VDD and the output, and a block of pull-down logic between the output and ground, with the PUN and PDN needing to be complementary (a CMOS inverter is drawn for the two input levels). A short “bottom line up front” list ties series and parallel switches to logical AND and OR, states what the PUN and the PDN each implement, and notes that PMOS needs a low input to turn on.

Example 1 (29-2) gives a PUN of two PMOS transistors beside each other over two NMOS in series and asks for the type of gate by filling in a truth table of which transistors conduct for each input pair. Example 2 (29-3) does the same for two PMOS in series over two NMOS side by side, and has you relate the PUN and PDN expressions through DeMorgan's law. A starred note observes that PMOS devices in series are not as good as NMOS in series, because of the larger resistance of PMOS, so designers try to avoid long series PMOS chains in complex gates. Example 3 (29-4) introduces the simplified (digital) symbols and asks for the logic function of a network written both from its PUN and from its PDN.

Lesson 28 notetaker: why NMOS pulls down and PMOS pulls up notetaker pp. 28-1 to 28-9

Summarized from the Lesson 28 notetaker

Lesson 28 treats each MOSFET as a switch. An NMOS is on when VGS>Vtn and has an on-resistance rDS=1/(kn′(W/L)(VGS−Vtn)); a PMOS is on when VSG>|Vtp|, and its source is always at the highest voltage. For a logic gate the output is pulled up to VDD for a logical 1 by a pull-up network and pulled down to ground for a logical 0 by a pull-down network.

Placing an NMOS in the pull-up network gives a degraded high level (at most VDD−Vtn), and a PMOS in the pull-down network gives a degraded low level (at least |Vtp|). The notetaker lists four key observations: only PMOS devices in the PUN; only NMOS devices in the PDN; a gate voltage at VDD turns an NMOS on; a gate voltage of 0 turns a PMOS on. Three inverter options follow (a resistor load, an NMOS load, and the complementary CMOS pair); the CMOS pair has no static power dissipation, only dissipation while switching. Lesson 28 has no assigned problems.

Switch-level model of the transistors §16.1.1, p. 1111; Fig. 16.1, p. 1112

Quoted · §16.1.1, p. 1111

Digital circuits utilize NMOS and PMOS transistors operating as switches. From Chapter 5, we know that a MOS transistor can operate as an on/off switch by using the gate voltage to operate the transistor in the triode region (“on” position) or in the cutoff region (“off” position).

Specifically, an NMOS transistor behaves as a closed switch, exhibiting a very small resistance (Ron or rDS) between its drain and source terminals when its gate voltage is “high,” usually at the power-supply level VDD, which represents a logic 1. Conversely, when the gate voltage is “low” (i.e., at or close to ground voltage), which represents a logic 0, the transistor is cut off, thus conducting zero current and acting as an open switch. This is illustrated in Fig. 16.1(a).

The PMOS transistor operates in a complementary fashion: To turn the transistor on, its gate voltage is made low (0 V or logic 0). Raising the gate voltage to VDD (logic 1) turns the PMOS transistor off. This is illustrated in Fig. 16.1(b).

We observe that the gate terminal of the MOSFET is used as the controlling node, and thus it is usually one of the input terminals of the logic gate.

General structure of CMOS logic §16.1.3, pp. 1112–1114
Quoted · §16.1.3, pp. 1112–1113

A CMOS logic circuit is in effect an extension, or a generalization, of the CMOS inverter: The inverter consists of an NMOS pull-down transistor and a PMOS pull-up transistor, operated by the input voltage in a complementary fashion. The CMOS logic gate consists of two networks: the pull-down network (PDN) constructed of NMOS transistors, and the pull-up network (PUN) constructed of PMOS transistors (see Fig. 16.3). The two networks are operated by the input variables, in a complementary fashion. Thus, for the three-input gate represented in Fig. 16.3, the PDN will conduct for all input combinations that require a low output (Y=0) and will then pull the output node down to ground, causing a zero voltage to appear at the output, vY=0. Simultaneously, the PUN will be off, and no direct dc path will exist between VDD and ground. On the other hand, all input combinations that call for a high output (Y=1) will cause the PUN to conduct, and the PUN will then pull the output node up to VDD, establishing an output voltage vY=VDD. Simultaneously, the PDN will be cut off, and again, no direct dc current path between VDD and ground will exist in the circuit.

How the networks conduct, with examples §16.1.3, pp. 1113–1115; Figs. 16.4 and 16.5

Quoted · pp. 1113–1114

Now, since the PDN comprises NMOS transistors, and since an NMOS transistor conducts when the signal at its gate is high, the PDN is activated (i.e., conducts) when the inputs are high. In a dual manner, the PUN comprises PMOS transistors, and a PMOS transistor conducts when the input signal at its gate is low; thus the PUN is activated when the inputs are low.

The PDN utilizes devices in parallel to form an OR function and devices in series to form an AND function; the same is true of the PUN. Here, the OR and AND notations refer to current flow or conduction. Figure 16.4 shows examples of PDNs. For the circuit in Fig. 16.4(a), QA will conduct when A is high (vA=VDD) and will then pull the output node down to ground (vY=0 V, Y=0). Similarly, QB conducts and pulls Y down when B is high. Thus Y will be low when A is high or B is high, which can be expressed as

Y‾=A+B

or equivalently

Y=A+B‾

The PDN in Fig. 16.4(b) will conduct only when A and B are both high simultaneously. Thus Y will be low when A is high and B is high,

Y‾=AB
Quoted · p. 1115

or equivalently

Y=AB‾

As a final example, the PDN in Fig. 16.4(c) will conduct and cause Y to be 0 when A is high or when B and C are both high, thus

Y‾=A+BC

or equivalently

Y=A+BC‾

Next consider the PUN examples shown in Fig. 16.5. The PUN in Fig. 16.5(a) will conduct and pull Y up to VDD (Y=1) when A is low or B is low, thus

Y=A‾+B‾

The PUN in Fig. 16.5(b) will conduct and produce a high output (vY=VDD, Y=1) only when A and B are both low, thus

Y=A‾B‾

Finally, the PUN in Fig. 16.5(c) will conduct and cause Y to be high (logic 1) if A is low or if B and C are both low; thus,

Y=A‾+B‾C‾
Expansion note: reading "Y = A + B" under a pull-up drawing

The expression printed under each drawing is the output of that network alone. Under a PDN it is the condition for Y‾ (the output being pulled low); under a PUN it is the condition for Y itself (the output being pulled high). That is why the PUN expressions contain bars on the inputs: a PMOS device turns the output high when its input is low.

The digital symbols p. 1115; Fig. 16.6

Quoted · p. 1115

Having developed an understanding and appreciation of the structure and operation of PDNs and PUNs, we are almost ready to consider complete CMOS gates. First, however, we need to get to know the alternative circuit symbols that digital-circuit designers almost universally use for MOS transistors. Figure 16.6 shows our usual symbols (left) and the corresponding “digital” symbols (right). Notice that the symbol for the PMOS transistor with a circle at the gate terminal is intended to indicate that the signal at the gate has to be low for the device to be activated (i.e., to conduct). Thus, in terms of logic-circuit terminology, the gate terminal of the PMOS transistor is an active low input. Besides indicating this property of PMOS devices, the digital symbols omit any indication of which of the device terminals is the source and which is the drain. This should cause no difficulty at this stage of our study; simply remember that for an NMOS transistor, the drain is the terminal at the higher voltage (current flows from drain to source), and for a PMOS transistor the source is the terminal at the higher voltage (current flows from source to drain). To be consistent with the literature, we will now use these modified symbols for MOS transistors in logic applications, except where our usual symbols help in understanding circuit operation.

Complete gates: NOR, NAND and a complex gate §§16.1.4–16.1.6, pp. 1116–1118

Quoted · §16.1.4, p. 1116

We first consider the CMOS gate that realizes the two-input NOR function

Y=A+B‾=A‾B‾
(16.1)

We can see that Y is to be low (PDN conducting) when A is high or B is high. Thus the PDN consists of two parallel NMOS devices with A and B as inputs [i.e., the circuit in Fig. 16.4(a)]. For the PUN, we note from the second expression in Eq. (16.1) that Y is to be high when A and B are both low. Thus the PUN consists of two series PMOS devices with A and B as the inputs [i.e., the circuit in Fig. 16.5(b)]. Putting the PDN and the PUN together gives the CMOS NOR gate shown in Fig. 16.7. Note that extension to a higher number of inputs is straightforward: For each additional input, an NMOS transistor is added in parallel with QNA and QNB, and a PMOS transistor is added in series with QPA and QPB.

Quoted · §16.1.5, pp. 1116–1117

The two-input NAND function is described by the Boolean expression

Y=AB‾=A‾+B‾
(16.2)

To synthesize the PDN, we consider the input combinations that require Y to be low: There is only one such combination, namely, A and B both high. Thus, the PDN simply comprises two NMOS transistors in series [such as the circuit in Fig. 16.4(b)]. To synthesize the PUN, we consider the input combinations that result in Y being high. These are found from the second expression in Eq. (16.2) as A low or B low. Thus, the PUN consists of two parallel PMOS transistors with A and B applied to their gates [such as the circuit in Fig. 16.5(a)]. Putting the PDN and PUN together results in the CMOS NAND gate implementation shown in Fig. 16.8. Note that extension to a higher number of inputs is straightforward: For each additional input, we add an NMOS transistor in series with QNA and QNB, and a PMOS transistor in parallel with QPA and QPB.

Obtaining the PUN from the PDN and vice versa §16.1.6–§16.1.7, pp. 1117–1118; Fig. 16.9

Quoted · §16.1.6, p. 1117

Consider next the more complex logic function

Y=A(B+CD)‾
(16.3)

Since Y‾=A(B+CD), we see that Y should be low for A high and simultaneously either B high or C and D both high, from which the PDN is directly obtained. To obtain the PUN, we need to express Y in terms of the complemented variables. We do this through repeated application of DeMorgan's law, as follows:

Y=A(B+CD)‾=A‾+B+CD‾=A‾+B‾CD‾=A‾+B‾(C‾+D‾)
(16.4)

Thus, Y is high for A low or B low and either C or D low. The corresponding complete CMOS circuit will be as shown in Fig. 16.9.

Quoted · §16.1.7, pp. 1117–1118

From the CMOS gate circuits considered thus far (e.g., that in Fig. 16.9), we observe that the PDN and the PUN are dual networks: Where a series branch exists in one, a parallel branch exists in the other. Thus, we can obtain one from the other, a process that can be simpler than having to synthesize each separately from the Boolean expression of the function. For instance, in the circuit of Fig. 16.9, we found it relatively easy to obtain the PDN, simply because we already had Y‾ in terms of the uncomplemented inputs. On the other hand, to obtain the PUN, we had to manipulate the given Boolean expression to express Y as a function of the complemented variables, the form convenient for synthesizing PUNs. Alternatively, we could have used this duality property to obtain the PUN from the PDN. The reader is urged to refer to Fig. 16.9 to convince herself that this is indeed possible.

We should, however, mention that at times it is not easy to obtain one of the two networks from the other using the duality property. For such cases, we would have to resort to a more rigorous process, which is beyond the scope of this book (see Kang, Leblebici, and Kim, 2016).

Expansion note: what "dual" means for a network

Two networks are duals when every series connection in one corresponds to a parallel connection in the other, and every parallel connection to a series one, with the same inputs on corresponding devices. Because the PDN conducts when the PUN does not, the pair covers every input combination exactly once.

Summary of the synthesis method and a worked example §16.1.9, pp. 1119–1121; Example 16.1

Quoted · §16.1.9, pp. 1119–1120

1. The PDN can be most directly synthesized by expressing Y‾ as a function of the uncomplemented variables. If complemented variables appear in this expression, additional inverters will be required to generate them.

2. The PUN can be most directly synthesized by expressing Y as a function of the complemented variables and then applying the uncomplemented variables to the gates of the PMOS transistors. If uncomplemented variables appear in the expression, additional inverters will be needed.

3. The PDN can be obtained from the PUN (and vice versa) using the duality property.

Quoted · Example 16.1 statement, p. 1120

Synthesize a CMOS logic circuit that implements the Boolean function

Y=A+B(C+D)‾
Quoted · Example 16.1 solution, pp. 1120–1121

To obtain the PDN we use

Y‾=A+B(C+D)

and note that Y‾ will be low when A is high or when [B(C+D)] is high. Thus we have two parallel networks. One consists of a single transistor with A supplied to its gate, and the second is a network composed of a transistor controlled by B in series with two parallel transistors controlled by C and D. The resulting PDN is shown in Fig. 16.11(a).

A question arises: Should the B transistor be placed closer to ground (with the C and D transistors closer to Y) or closer to Y? From a logic standpoint, both are valid solutions.

To obtain the PUN we use deMorgan's law on the given expression for Y to obtain

Y=A‾(B‾+C‾D‾)

which leads to the circuit in Fig. 16.11(b). Here again, we may exchange the positions of the C and D transistors with no effect on the logic behavior. Finally, the complete circuit can be obtained by combining the PDN and the PUN shown in Fig. 16.11.

Problem 16.7 Lesson 29 · p. 1145 · §16.1

Given a pull-up network, find the matching pull-down network, the complete CMOS gate and its Boolean function.

Problem statement

16.7 Find the PDN that corresponds to the PUN shown in Fig. P16.7, and hence the complete CMOS logic circuit. What is the Boolean function realized?

Similar to 16.7 given PUN, find the PDN, the whole gate and the function · §16.1

Same kind of question with a different pull-up network.

Similar problem (new network)

Find the PDN that corresponds to the PUN shown below, and hence the complete CMOS logic circuit. What is the Boolean function realized?

Step 1 · When does the PUN conduct?

A PMOS transistor conducts when its gate is low. Series devices form an AND and parallel devices an OR, so the PUN pulls Y up when A is low and B is low and (C is low or D is low):

Y=A‾B‾(C‾+D‾)
Step 2 · Express Y‾ with uncomplemented variables

The PDN is most directly built from Y‾ in terms of the uncomplemented inputs (§16.1.9, item 1). Complement both sides and apply DeMorgan's law as in Eq. (16.4), working from the inside out:

Y‾=A‾B‾(C‾+D‾)‾=A+B+C‾+D‾‾=A+B+CD
Step 3 · Read off the PDN

Y‾ is high, so the PDN conducts, when A is high or B is high or (C and D are both high). Three branches in parallel: a single NMOS for A, a single NMOS for B, and a series pair for C and D. This agrees with duality (§16.1.7): the series chain A-B-(C or D) of the PUN becomes the parallel arrangement A, B, (C and D), and the parallel C, D pair becomes a series pair.

Step 4 · Complete circuit and function
Y=A+B+CD‾

Check: for every input combination exactly one network conducts (all 16 rows were confirmed in the saved script), so no direct dc path from VDD to ground exists. Device count: 4 PMOS + 4 NMOS = 8.

Answers (similar problem)
PDNNMOS A, NMOS B and the series pair NMOS C-D, all three branches in parallel
Boolean functionY=A+B+CD‾

Expansion note: why the PUN expression has bars on the inputs

A PMOS device turns the output high when its gate input is low, so each PMOS device contributes the complement of its input to the condition for Y. The PDN works the other way: an NMOS device contributes its input as is, to the condition for Y‾.

Lesson 29 notetaker: synthesizing from expressions and truth tables notetaker pp. 29-4 to 29-8

Summarized from the Lesson 29 notetaker

Example 3 (29-4) works from a drawn network to its logic function, once from the PUN and once from the PDN, using the simplified symbols; a margin line recalls that DeMorgan's law is applied by reversing the inputs, swapping AND and OR, and reversing the total.

Example 4 (29-5, 29-6) realizes the PUN and PDN for Y=A(B+CD)‾ in steps. Step 1 works first with the PUN: apply DeMorgan's law as three sub-steps (1) complement each input, (2) swap AND and OR (inside to outside), (3) complement; the PUN works with the complemented variables. Step 2 synthesizes the PDN from Y‾: the PDN works with the uncomplemented variables, and a starred recall note says the PDN can be found from the logic of the PUN expression by complementing the variables, working inside out and swapping AND and OR.

Example 5 (29-7) builds the PUN and PDN from a truth table: review minterms (ANDs of inputs where Y=1) and maxterms (ORs of inputs where Y=0), express Y and Y‾ as sums of products, then create the PUN (using complemented inputs) and the PDN (using uncomplemented inputs). Page 29-8 asks how to create the PDN using the dual (swap AND and OR) and how many transistors are required, then begins noise margins, which belong to the next lesson and not to this problem.

Switch-level model and structure of CMOS logic §§16.1.1–16.1.3, pp. 1111–1115

Summarized (the full quoted passages and Figs. 16.1 to 16.6 are in the Problem 16.5 section)

An NMOS transistor acts as a closed switch when its gate is high (logic 1, VDD) and an open switch when the gate is low. A PMOS transistor is the complement: closed for a low gate, open for a high gate. A CMOS gate is a PDN of NMOS devices from the output to ground plus a PUN of PMOS devices from VDD to the output, driven by the same inputs. Exactly one network conducts for any input combination (p. 1113). In both networks, series devices form an AND and parallel devices an OR of conduction (p. 1114).

The complex gate and duality §16.1.6–§16.1.7, pp. 1117–1118; Fig. 16.9

Quoted · §16.1.6, p. 1117

Consider next the more complex logic function

Y=A(B+CD)‾

(16.4)

Quoted · §16.1.7, pp. 1117–1118

We should, however, mention that at times it is not easy to obtain one of the two networks from the other using the duality property. For such cases, we would have to resort to a more rigorous process, which is beyond the scope of this book (see Kang, Leblebici, and Kim, 2016).

Expansion note: going from the PUN to the PDN

The book's complex-gate example goes the other way (PDN first, then the PUN by DeMorgan's law), but the same two routes apply in reverse. You can read the PUN's condition directly and then complement it, or you can swap series and parallel in the drawing. The book notes both are valid and that each should agree with the other.

Summary of the synthesis method and a worked example §16.1.9, pp. 1119–1121; Example 16.1

Quoted · §16.1.9, pp. 1119–1120

1. The PDN can be most directly synthesized by expressing Y‾ as a function of the uncomplemented variables. If complemented variables appear in this expression, additional inverters will be required to generate them.

2. The PUN can be most directly synthesized by expressing Y as a function of the complemented variables and then applying the uncomplemented variables to the gates of the PMOS transistors. If uncomplemented variables appear in the expression, additional inverters will be needed.

Summarized · Example 16.1, pp. 1120–1121 (full text and Fig. 16.11 are in the Problem 16.5 section)

The book synthesizes the gate for Y=A+B(C+D)‾: it reads the PDN directly from Y‾=A+B(C+D) (two parallel networks: one transistor for A, and a series chain of B with a parallel C, D pair), then applies DeMorgan's law to get Y in the complemented variables for the PUN, and joins the two networks. It notes that the positions of the B transistor relative to the C, D pair may be swapped: from a logic standpoint both are valid.
